candidates.title: Per-Query Monte Carlo Tree Search over Agent Routing Guided by an Outcome-Derived Process Reward Model
candidates.summary: This proposal targets multi-agent orchestration. Instead of a fixed workflow or a single learned RL policy, it plans which specialist agent acts next for each individual query. The method runs UCT-style tree search in which each node is a shared task state and each edge calls one agent (planner, coder, debugger, critic, tool caller). Nodes are scored by a step-level process reward model. Its labels come automatically from Monte Carlo rollout outcomes, so no human annotation is needed. Validation would test whether this search beats static, RL-trained and offline-searched orchestrators on coding, scientific-reasoning and visualization benchmarks at matched token budgets.
candidates.gap: The puppeteer orchestrator learns one reactive routing policy through RL and does no lookahead at inference time. AFlow and ADAS search offline for one workflow per dataset, which is then fixed for every query. LATS and RAP apply MCTS only to the reasoning or action steps of a single agent, not to routing decisions among heterogeneous agents. Process reward models are trained and used for math steps and agent actions, but none of these works uses them as value functions for multi-agent routing.
candidates.approach: 1) Define the shared state as the task, the artifacts produced so far and the execution feedback; define actions as invoking one agent from a fixed pool. 2) Collect rollouts and label each intermediate state with the fraction of its continuations that succeed, following the Math-Shepherd and OVM recipe for automatic process labels. Fine-tune a small open LLM such as Qwen3 or Llama 3 into an orchestration value model. 3) At test time, run UCT with this value model as the leaf evaluator and execution signals (unit tests, rendering success) as terminal reward. Penalize the search for token cost.
candidates.evaluation: Baselines: static chains in the MetaGPT and ChatDev style, AutoGen group chat, the puppeteer RL orchestrator, the best AFlow workflow, single-agent LATS, and Self-Refine. Benchmarks: HumanEval and MBPP (pass@1), SciBench (accuracy), MatPlotBench (score from a vision LLM judge). Report accuracy against total tokens and cost. Ablations: search guided by an outcome-only reward model versus a process reward model, LLM-as-judge values versus the learned value model, and search depth and width.

candidates.title: DAgger Distillation of Search-Based Orchestrators into Lightweight Routers Without Causal Confusion
candidates.summary: Search-based multi-agent orchestration may be accurate but is expensive. This proposal distills a costly tree-search orchestrator, used as the expert, into a small routing policy. It replaces plain behavioral cloning with DAgger-style on-policy aggregation: the router runs its own trajectories and the expert relabels the states it visits. To avoid causal misidentification, it trains on a compact predicate-based state abstraction instead of the full conversation history, and runs targeted expert queries when routing is uncertain. Validation would measure how much of the expert's accuracy the router retains at a fraction of the cost, and its robustness on out-of-distribution task families.
candidates.gap: Orchestrators trained by RL or by search are costly. The obvious shortcut, imitating search traces offline, is behavioral cloning, which suffers compounding errors under the router's own state distribution. Routers that see the full message history also risk causal confusion: they may latch onto superficial cues such as message length or which agent spoke last. No cited multi-agent work uses imitation learning with these guarantees, or a deliberately reduced input, for routing.
candidates.approach: 1) Use an MCTS-plus-value-model orchestrator as the expert. 2) Build the router's input from discrete predicates (for example, tests failing, plot rendered, plan exists, and the last tool error type), using the representation style of policy graphs. 3) Train the router with DAgger: roll out the current router, query the expert at the visited states, add those labels to the dataset and retrain. Cap the number of expert queries by router entropy. 4) Compare a full-history input with the predicate input to check for causal confusion.
candidates.evaluation: Baselines: the expert search orchestrator (upper bound), behavioral cloning on expert traces, the puppeteer RL orchestrator, static workflows, and an LLM zero-shot router. Measures: task success on HumanEval, MBPP, SciBench and MatPlotBench, and transfer to held-out ALFWorld or WebArena tasks; expert queries and tokens per task; the accuracy gap between the router and the expert as DAgger iterations increase. Run the input-ablation test that shows whether adding more history hurts out-of-distribution performance.

candidates.title: Intention-Aware Policy Graphs for Explaining and Auditing LLM Multi-Agent Orchestrators
candidates.summary: This proposal addresses the compound opacity of LLM multi-agent systems by adapting policy-graph explainability, built for reinforcement-learning agents, to LLM orchestrators. From logged orchestration traces, it abstracts states into discrete predicates and builds a probabilistic policy graph that records which agent is called under which conditions. It computes intention scores for sub-goals such as 'produce passing code', which support answering what the orchestrator wants, how it plans to get there, and why it chose an action. Explanation fidelity would be validated by deploying a surrogate orchestrator derived from the graph and comparing its behaviour and task success with the original. The graphs would also be used to flag irrational or redundant routing.
candidates.gap: Policy graphs and intention-aware explanations have been shown only for RL agents in cooperative game environments. Work on LLM multi-agent systems, including the evolved cyclic structures of the RL-trained orchestrator and pruned communication graphs, reports performance but offers no faithful, checkable explanation of routing decisions. The radiology ethics analysis names this compound opacity as unsolved.
candidates.approach: 1) Log the traces of trained orchestrators (an RL puppeteer and a search-based orchestrator) on coding, scientific and visualization tasks. 2) Define predicates over task state and agent outputs; estimate transition and action probabilities to build the policy graph. 3) Compute intention scores for user-specified desires and generate answers to what, how and why questions. 4) Derive a surrogate policy from the graph and run it in place of the original orchestrator. 5) Use low-intention or cyclic regions of the graph to detect wasted agent calls, and test whether pruning them keeps accuracy while reducing tokens.
candidates.evaluation: Fidelity: action agreement between the surrogate and the original orchestrator, and the gap in task success (pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP, MatPlotBench score). Intention measures: attributed intention and intention precision, reported as a function of predicate granularity. Explanation quality: human or LLM-judge ratings of answers to why questions, with judge agreement checked against humans. Efficiency audit: the token reduction and change in accuracy after pruning guided by the graph, compared with AgentPrune.
